info.bio:
Nació en Liverpool, Reino Unido, 25 de febrero de 1943 - † Los Angeles, Estados Unidos, 29 de noviembre de 2001. Uno de los cuatro genios de Liverpool, integrante de la banda de música más importante e influyente del siglo XX: The Beatles. Como guitarrista, dueño de un estilo único, como compositor creador de canciones tan extrordinarias como las de sus compañeros Lennon-McCartney.

George formó parte desde el principio de The Beatles, de la mano de Paul se unió al grupo, y ya no lo abandonaría hasta su disolución.

scenes.name: The Beatles
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Su primer single, «Love Me Do», entró en las listas el 11 de octubre de 1962, días antes de la crisis de los misiles. En 1963 provocaron una histeria femenina sin precedentes, rompieron la deferencia de los cincuenta y, por un breve tiempo, el sistema de clases: una revolución hecha con una melodía, un flequillo y un «yeah yeah yeah». En abril de 1964 ocuparon los cinco primeros puestos de Billboard, dispararon la venta de singles y convirtieron Gran Bretaña en la «Isla Pop». Su ejemplo obligaba a componer material propio. En 1966 hay pausas súbitas dentro del impulso imparable de «Rain».

scenes.name: La India en el pop: sitar y raga rock
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: La música india se convirtió en la metáfora sonora central del LSD: el dron del sitar y la longitud de las piezas reproducían la dislocación del tiempo, el timbre vibraba en el cuerpo, había un impulso religioso y, a oídos occidentales, ni ego ni formato de tres minutos. Entró en el pop con «See My Friends» de los Kinks, «Heart Full of Soul» de los Yardbirds y la banda sonora de Help!, donde los Beatles descubrieron el sitar poco después de su primer ácido. Jim Dickson, mánager de los Byrds, tenía relación con World Pacific, que grababa a Ravi Shankar (Portrait of a Genius, Sound of the Sitar); Tony Hall recomendaba vivir con sus discos y Harrison quedó deslumbrado al verlo en el Festival Hall. En 1966 llegaron «Eight Miles High», «Shapes of Things», «Paint It, Black» y «Tomorrow Never Knows».

scenes.name: Cantautores de los setenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: James Taylor se convierte, misteriosamente, en el prototipo del cantautor de los setenta; Carole King, Carly Simon y Don McLean, sobrevalorados. Las innovaciones llegan del oeste: Randy Newman y sus viñetas urbanas con fusión de estilos populares, Shawn Phillips, J.J. Cale y su estilo «laid-back», Gram Parsons, Emmylou Harris, Roger McGuinn, Jackson Browne (Late For The Sky) y, sobre todo, Tom Waits, discípulo de Beefheart y cronista de marginados (Swordfishtrombones, Rain Dogs). Excéntricos como Todd Rundgren y Annette Peacock; en Gran Bretaña, Peter Hammill, Anthony Moore, Richard Thompson, Robert Calvert, John Cale, Kevin Coyne, Elton John y los ex Beatles. El realismo de Bruce Springsteen, verdadero heredero de Woody Guthrie y del blues, y la escuela italiana de cantautores (De André, Guccini, Battisti, Sorrenti).

podcast.title: Departure from The Beatles - Get Back Sessions (1969)
podcast.body: George Harrison famously left The Beatles "in a huff" during the 1969 *Get Back Sessions*. This incident highlights the internal drama within The Beatles, which is compared to the interpersonal conflicts of Fleetwood Mac. "George Harrison, who infamously left the group in a huff during 1969's Get Back Sessions."

podcast.title: Bankrolling "Shanghai Surprise" (1986)
podcast.body: George Harrison's production company bankrolled the film "Shanghai Surprise," starring Sean Penn and Madonna. The movie's significant box office failure nearly led to Harrison's bankruptcy. "Shanghai Surprise, her exotic adventure with her husband Sean, flopped so hard, it nearly bankrupted former Beatles George Harrison, whose production company had bankrolled the film."

podcast.title: Fear of Religious References in Music
podcast.body: Harrison anticipated public backlash when writing "My Sweet Lord" due to his intention to use explicit religious terms like "Lord" and "God," noting that "Many people fear the words Lord and God. It makes them angry for some strange reason." This highlights the perceived risk of overtly religious themes in popular music. "I would be committing myself publicly and I anticipated that a lot of people might get weird about it."

podcast.title: Inspiration for Sun King - Fleetwood Mac's Albatross
podcast.body: George Harrison admitted in later interviews that The Beatles' song "Sun King," written by John Lennon and featured on the *Abbey Road* album, was inspired by Fleetwood Mac's then-recent British number 1 hit instrumental, "Albatross." This acknowledges a direct musical influence from Fleetwood Mac on The Beatles. "In later interviews, guitarist George Harrison admitted that Sun King was inspired by the then recent Fleetwood Mac hit."

podcast.body: George Harrison notably played a Gibson Les Paul Custom during the recording of "While My Guitar Gently Weeps." podcast.title: Persuaded Lennon on "Sexy Sadie" Title
podcast.body: George Harrison persuaded John Lennon to change the title of his song from "Maharishi" to "Sexy Sadie," noting that the new title had the same number of syllables. "Lennon wanted to call the song Maharishi, but George Harrison persuaded him to go with Sexy Sadie, which had the same number of syllables."

podcast.title: Plagiarism of "He's So Fine"
podcast.body: George Harrison's "My Sweet Lord" was found by a judge to have unintentionally plagiarized "He's So Fine," a 1963 song by The Chiffons, written by Ronnie Mack. John Lennon, however, expressed skepticism about the unintentional nature of the plagiarism. It was also considered "a bit odd that Phil Spector did not pick up on this." "Musically though, I would be remiss to gloss over the fact that Harrison plagiarized he's so fine, written by Ronnie Mack for the chiffons in 1963."

His debut solo album, *All Things Must Pass*, was a significant statement to establish his independent musical identity. "Who was George Harrison if he was no longer a beetle?"

xref.title: 1958 Percy Phillips Home Recording – "That'll Be the Day" / "In Spite of All the Danger"
xref.body: An ultra-rare, two-sided 78 RPM disc from 1958, recorded by John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, pianist John Lowe, and drummer Colin Hanton at the home of Percy Phillips, who specialized in "down and dirty" recordings in his front room. Side one features Buddy Holly's "That'll Be the Day," and side two contains "In Spite of All the Danger," the first-ever Lennon-McCartney recording. This record is owned by Paul McCartney and is estimated to be worth at least 100,000 pounds if it were ever to be sold. "The result was a two-sided 78 RPM disc with Buddy Holly's That'll Be the Day on Side One, and the first ever Lennon McCartney recording on the other, in spite of all the danger."

xref.title: The Residents (Shreveport LA, 1969) – No Known Members; Hardy W. Fox Died 2018 Listed as Co-Founder; George Harrison and Claypool Denied
xref.body: The Residents are an art collective that originated in Shreveport, Louisiana in 1969. By 1971 they were performing in San Francisco. They have never shown their faces or listed any band members — their only point of contact is a company called Cryptic Music. When their debut album Meet the Residents was released in 1974 (parodying the Beatles' Meet the Beatles), some fans believed they were actually the Beatles in disguise. Hardy W. Fox — who claimed to have been a Resident — died in 2018 with his obituary listing him as co-founder and primary songwriter. Other names tied to the band include Homer Cook (unconfirmed), Jay Clem (maybe), and "Charles Boebuck" (apparently a pseudonym for Fox). Contrary to rumors, George Harrison, Les Claypool of Primus, and no member of Devo has ever been in the band. "I can tell you, though, contrary to rumors, George Harrison less clay pool of primus, and no one from Devo has ever been in the residence."

xref.title: George Harrison on Ringo's Death Threat (1990)
xref.body: In 1990, George Harrison recounted a specific death threat against Ringo Starr during The Beatles' 1964 Montreal visit. He stated that a Montreal newspaper reported someone intended to kill Ringo, possibly because they disliked his nose or because he was perceived as "the most British of the Beatles." "A Montreal newspaper reported that somebody was going to kill Ringo because they didn't like his nose or something, because he was probably the most British of the Beatles."

xref.title: "Now and Then" - AI-Assisted Song (2020s)
xref.body: The Beatles created a brand new song, "Now and Then," utilizing artificial intelligence technology. Film director Peter Jackson was able to isolate John Lennon's vocals from a "bad sounding 1978 cassette demo," allowing Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr to add new parts, alongside George Harrison's contributions from a 1995 session. "But then we can point to what the Beatles did with AI and the song Now and Then, using brand new technology. Film director Peter Jackson was able to isolate John's vocals from a bad sounding 1978 cassette demo."

xref.title: "Wonderwall" Title Interpretations
xref.body: The title "Wonderwall" has multiple potential origins and meanings according to Noel Gallagher. Initially, it was about his then-girlfriend Meg Matthews. After their 2001 divorce, it morphed into being about an imaginary person who would save him. He later connected it to George Harrison's 1968 album "Wonder Wall Music." Additionally, it may refer to a brick wall at Rockfield Studios where he would sit and play guitar, potentially seeing it as his "songwriting Wonder Wall." "The brick construction was perhaps his songwriting Wonder Wall."

xref.title: Developing Mop Top Haircut (Astrid Kircher)
xref.body: About a year after the initial cut by Yurgen Volmer, during The Beatles' extended residency in Hamburg, Astrid Kircher regularly cut their hair into this new look. She first applied the cut to Stu Sutcliffe, then George Harrison, and finally John Lennon and Paul McCartney. Within two years, as The Beatles became the biggest band globally, their haircuts were nearly as famous as their music, solidifying long hair on men as a lasting trend. "She first gave the cut to Stu, and then George, and then finally John and Paul."

xref.title: Esteemed Fans and Original Songwriting
xref.body: Before their breakup in 1975, Fanny garnered a significant following that included David Bowie, John Lennon, George Harrison, and Sly Stone. They released five major label albums and notably wrote all their own songs, a rare feat for female artists at the time. "David Bowie, John and George from The Beatles, Slice Stone, and a ton of other big names became huge fans. They released five major label albums and they wrote all their own songs, which is something almost no female artists did back in those days."

xref.title: Extensive Session Work
xref.body: Jim Gordon was a highly prolific drummer, contributing to literally hundreds of songs for a wide array of prominent artists including George Harrison, Joe Cocker, Dave Mason, Gordon Lightfoot, Harry Nilsson, Frank Zappa, Art Garfunkel, Traffic, and Steely Dan. He even contributed to the first Muppet movie. "Gordon could be heard on literally hundreds of songs."

xref.title: Highly Respected by Famous Musicians
xref.body: Fanny garnered a significant following among prominent musicians, with huge fans including David Bowie, John Lennon and George Harrison from The Beatles, and Sly Stone, among many other big names in the industry. David Bowie even sent them a fan letter and spoke highly of them in interviews. "Before they broke up in 1975, David Bowie, John and George from the Beatles, Slice Stone, and a ton of other big names became huge fans."

xref.title: Iconic Vox AC30 Chord
xref.body: The most famous single chord played through a Vox AC30 involves John Lennon on a Gibson J130E (an acoustic-electric) and George Harrison on a 12-string Rickenbacker 360-12. This specific combination of guitars and amplifier was crucial for achieving their distinctive "jangly" sound. "The only way to achieve that sound was with those guitars and Vox amps."

xref.title: Individual Members' Solo Careers
xref.body: Following The Beatles' decision to stop touring in 1966 and their eventual breakup, individual members — John Lennon, George Harrison, Paul McCartney, and Ringo Starr — all went on to play solo shows in Canada. "And while the group would never play Canada again, the country would still see individual members over the next few years."

xref.title: Wall of Sound Production Method
xref.body: Phil Spector was known for his immersive production through his "Wall of Sound" methods, developed in the early 1960s. These techniques typically resulted in upbeat, high-energy, and danceable songs. When working with George Harrison, however, he adapted this method to a more subdued style.
